page_placements.theme: Refusal direction vs directions for other non-answering behaviours (abstention, hedging, incapability, bail, derailing, privacy refusal): overlap and specificity

record.file_problem: Repository metadata, README, and file list only; the referenced paper and result files were not read. The README reports results, but does not provide the underlying per-model refusal counts.
record.tranche_reason: The repository adapts the original direction-finding and intervention method to hedging and reports hedging outcomes. It does not test the claimed harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. Its separate refusal check ablates a hedge direction, not the direction named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The reported ablation and addition results concern hedging, a different behavior from refusal, and therefore do not test V1–V8. The README also reports that ablating the hedge direction changes refusal counts by at most four among 32 requests, with changes in both directions; it does not provide per-model counts or baseline refusal rates. The README states that further details are in files that were not read.
record.test_reason: The study applies Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means, ablation and addition method to hedging, a different behaviour. The direction is built from hedged versus direct prompts, not harmful versus harmless instructions. Its only refusal measurement ablates the hedge direction, not the refusal direction; the README says the code deliberately does not ablate the refusal direction. No result bears on whether any version V1–V8 holds for the refusal direction, so this is the method used as a tool on another construct.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right but should add two points. First, the real direction beats every shuffled-label direction under ablation in five of the seven models. Second, some shuffled directions match the addition effect, so the authors say they are more confident the direction is necessary for hedging than sufficient. They also caution that the direction may encode question type (contested vs clear-cut) and that the keyword judge overstates effects, addition most.
record.recipe_differences: Repository for a course research project adapting the original direction method to hedging. It extracts a difference between hedge-labeled and direct-answer prompts and intervenes on that direction; it does not extract the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. The README describes the method and reports results, but the code was not run.
record.method_sensitivity: The README reports that addition sometimes performs similarly to shuffled-label directions, that the keyword judge overstates effects relative to human labels (especially addition), and that Qwen2.5 held-out AUROC rises from 0.84 at 1.5B to 0.95 at 32B. It also says the best layer stays at about two thirds of model depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the hedge direction turns 89–100% of held-out hedged answers direct across seven instruct models, against 5–17% for random directions (keyword judge). Adding it makes 21–52% of direct answers hedge, against 4–14% for random directions. Some shuffled-label directions match the addition effect. By human labels, ablation gives 75% vs 18% and addition 49% vs 31%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In instruct models, hedging is necessarily mediated by a difference-in-means direction (hedged minus direct prompts). Adding that direction is a weaker and less specific cause of hedging.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the hedge direction changed refusal of 32 JailbreakBench requests by at most four, up in some models and down in others. Exact counts are not in the README.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The hedge direction is largely separate from the mechanism that produces refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5, held-out AUROC of the hedge direction rises from 0.84 (1.5B) to 0.95 (32B). The best layer stays near two thirds of model depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear separability of hedging increases with model scale within a family.

record.problems: The README calls the keyword judge a proxy and the largest error source; human ratings indicate it overstates both intervention effects, especially addition. The text advises checking judge accuracy per model and running multiple seeds, but does not report those checks for the study results summarized here. The refusal check lacks per-model counts and stated uncertainty in the README. General capability preservation is not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the results reported in the README. Other results and details referenced in results/RESULTS.md, model report files, and the paper were not read.
record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. No verdict is given because no row measures the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. The README says the refusal test can add a cosine with the refusal direction when harmless prompts are supplied, but it reports no such value. The README also notes that Qwen switches to Chinese when the hedge direction is ablated on harmful requests, and keeps refusing there. Per-model refusal counts are in report.md and results.json, which were not read. Even so, they would concern hedge-direction ablation and would not link to any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study finds a hedging direction rather than a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction; it does not test removal or addition of the claimed refusal direction or preservation of general capabilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No test of jailbreak suppression of the claimed refusal direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, model variants, or base and instruct stages for the claimed refusal direction.
No test of how refusal training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.

relation.reason: The method is used as a tool for a different behaviour. No result bears on whether a harmful-minus-harmless direction mediates refusal. The optional cosine with the refusal direction is not reported.

tranche.reason: Uses Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means, ablation and addition method for hedging (hedged vs direct prompts). It reports only results for the hedge direction. Its refusal test ablates the hedge direction, and the README says the code deliberately does not remove the refusal direction.

source_check.notes: The text is the README only. The paper PDF and per-model report.md files are not included, so per-model refusal counts cannot be checked. All headline rates are keyword-judge rates; on hand labels, ablation is 75% vs 18% random and addition 49% vs 31%. When the hedge direction is ablated on harmful requests, Qwen switches to Chinese but keeps refusing; the refusal scorer adds non-English refusal phrases to the paper's list. The record's authors_conclusion paraphrase matches the README.

statements.correction: Ablation 89-100% vs random 5-17% is by keyword judge on held-out test splits. On 93 hand-labelled test answers (pooled across models): ablation turns 75% of hedged answers direct vs 18% for random directions; the judge matched the human labels on 78% (kappa 0.56); the authors say the judge overstates both effects. The refusal change of at most 4 of 32 comes from ablating the hedge direction, not the refusal direction.
statements.problem: All numbers match: 7 instruct models, ablation 89-100%, random 5-17%, 32 JailbreakBench requests, refusal change of at most 4. But the rates are keyword-judge rates, and the authors say this judge overstates the effects. The statement presents them as actual conversion rates.
